question: The "chord line" of an aerofoil is best described as:

options.text: A curved line following the upper camber of the wing
A straight line joining the leading edge to the trailing edge
The line traced by the wingtip vortex
A line perpendicular to the wing's leading edge

explanation: The chord line is a straight reference line from the leading edge to the trailing edge of an aerofoil section. Both angle of attack and camber are measured against this line.

question: An aerofoil's "camber" refers to:

options.text: The straight line from the leading edge to the trailing edge
The curvature of the mean line drawn halfway between the upper and lower surfaces, relative to the chord line
The thickness of the aerofoil at its thickest point
The angle between the chord line and the relative airflow

explanation: Camber describes how much the aerofoil's mean camber line curves away from the straight chord line. A symmetrical aerofoil has a mean camber line that coincides with the chord line — zero camber.

question: As angle of attack is increased, below the stalling angle, on a conventional cambered aerofoil, the center of pressure typically:

options.text: Moves forward, toward the leading edge
Moves aft, toward the trailing edge
Remains fixed at the quarter-chord point at all times
Moves outward toward the wingtip

explanation: On a cambered aerofoil, increasing angle of attack below the stall generally moves the center of pressure forward as more lift is generated further ahead on the wing.

question: At and beyond the stalling angle of attack, the center of pressure on a conventional cambered aerofoil:

options.text: Continues moving forward, exactly as it did below the stall
Moves rapidly aft, producing a nose-down pitching moment
Moves outward to the wingtip
Stops moving entirely

explanation: Once the airflow separates at the stall, lift is lost mainly toward the rear of the wing, and the center of pressure moves rapidly aft — the opposite of its pre-stall trend — producing a nose-down pitching moment that tends to reduce angle of attack on its own.

question: The "aerodynamic center" of an aerofoil is the point about which:

options.text: Lift always acts, identically to the center of pressure
The pitching moment coefficient remains essentially constant with changing angle of attack
The center of gravity must always be located
The center of pressure is fixed regardless of speed

explanation: Unlike the center of pressure, which moves with angle of attack, the aerodynamic center (close to the quarter-chord point in subsonic flow) is defined as the point about which the pitching moment coefficient stays essentially constant as angle of attack changes — a fixed reference point rather than a moving one.

question: Increasing an aerofoil's thickness-to-chord ratio, other things being equal, tends to:

options.text: Increase CLmax and improve low-speed handling, at the cost of more drag and a lower critical Mach number
Decrease CLmax and reduce drag
Have no effect on critical Mach number
Always improve high-speed performance

explanation: A thicker aerofoil section generally provides more structural depth and a higher maximum lift coefficient, useful at low speed, but it also accelerates airflow over the upper surface more, increasing drag and lowering the critical Mach number — a classic low-speed/high-speed design trade-off.

question: A generously rounded leading edge radius on an aerofoil, compared with a sharp one, tends to:

options.text: Delay the onset of leading-edge flow separation, improving low-speed and high angle-of-attack behaviour
Only ever improve performance at supersonic speed
Increase the critical Mach number
Have no aerodynamic significance

explanation: A rounded leading edge lets airflow turn onto the upper surface more gently across a wider range of angle of attack before separating, which is why subsonic wings favour it. Sharp leading edges, by contrast, are favoured on supersonic wings, where a rounded edge would instead promote a strong, drag-producing bow shock.

question: Over the linear portion of the lift-versus-angle-of-attack curve, below the stall, increasing angle of attack by a fixed increment:

options.text: Produces a progressively smaller increase in lift coefficient each time
Produces an essentially constant, proportional increase in lift coefficient
Produces no change in lift coefficient
Always produces a decrease in lift coefficient

explanation: Below the stall, an aerofoil's lift coefficient rises essentially linearly with angle of attack — a constant lift curve slope — which is what makes the sudden departure from that straight line at the stall so distinct and important.

question: For a cambered aerofoil, the angle of attack at which lift is zero (the "zero-lift angle") is typically:

options.text: Exactly zero degrees
A small negative angle, because a cambered aerofoil still produces some lift at zero angle of attack
Always a positive angle greater than the stalling angle
Undefined for any real aerofoil

explanation: Camber lets an aerofoil generate lift even at zero angle of attack, so the angle of attack has to be reduced to a small negative value before lift actually reaches zero. A symmetrical aerofoil, by contrast, has a zero-lift angle of exactly zero degrees.

question: A conventional cambered aerofoil, considered alone, typically produces a pitching moment about its aerodynamic center that is:

options.text: Nose-up (positive)
Nose-down (negative), which is why a horizontal tailplane is needed to balance the aircraft in trimmed flight
Zero at every angle of attack
Dependent only on airspeed, not aerofoil shape

explanation: A cambered wing on its own produces a nose-down pitching moment about its aerodynamic center. In a complete aircraft, the horizontal tailplane normally produces a small download to balance this moment about the center of gravity in trimmed flight.

question: A symmetrical aerofoil, whose upper and lower surfaces are mirror images about the chord line, has:

options.text: A strongly cambered mean line and a pitching moment that varies greatly with angle of attack
Zero camber, a mean camber line that coincides with the chord line, and, in subsonic flow, an essentially zero pitching moment about its aerodynamic center at any angle of attack
A zero-lift angle of attack that is always a large negative value
No aerodynamic center of its own

explanation: Because a symmetrical aerofoil's upper and lower surfaces mirror each other, its mean camber line lies exactly on the chord line, giving zero camber, a zero-lift angle of exactly zero degrees, and — unlike a cambered section — essentially no pitching moment about its aerodynamic center.

question: A "reflex" camber line, curving back the other way near the trailing edge instead of continuing in one direction, is used mainly to:

options.text: Increase the nose-down pitching moment a conventional cambered section would otherwise produce
Reduce or reverse the nose-down pitching moment, which is useful on a tailless aircraft that has no separate tailplane to balance it
Increase maximum lift coefficient beyond that of an ordinary cambered aerofoil
Eliminate the aerofoil's zero-lift angle of attack entirely

explanation: An ordinary cambered aerofoil produces a nose-down pitching moment that a tailplane normally balances. A reflex trailing edge counters that moment within the aerofoil section itself, which is why tailless and flying-wing designs, lacking a separate tailplane, often use reflexed sections.

question: In aerofoil nomenclature, "upper camber" and "lower camber" refer to:

options.text: The curvature of the upper surface and the lower surface respectively, each measured relative to the chord line
The two endpoints of the mean camber line
The thickness of the aerofoil measured at the upper and lower surfaces
Two different names for exactly the same single quantity

explanation: An aerofoil's overall camber is really the average of two separate curves — the upper surface's curvature and the lower surface's curvature, each described relative to the straight chord line — which is what "upper camber" and "lower camber" name individually.

question: An aerofoil's "thickness distribution" describes:

options.text: How thickness varies along the chord from leading edge to trailing edge, which sets where the maximum thickness point lies and how quickly the surface accelerates the airflow
The single ratio obtained by dividing maximum thickness by chord length
The distance between the chord line and the mean camber line
How camber varies from wing root to wingtip

explanation: Thickness ratio is a single number; thickness distribution is the shape that number comes from — where along the chord the aerofoil is thickest and how the surface tapers away from that point, which affects pressure distribution and stall behaviour as much as the ratio itself does.

question: On an aerofoil section, the "leading edge" and "trailing edge" are:

options.text: The foremost point, where the chord line begins, and the rearmost point, where it ends
Both located at the point of maximum thickness
Interchangeable terms describing the same point on the section
Defined only relative to the wingtip, not to the chord line

explanation: The chord line is drawn from the leading edge, the forward-most point of the section, to the trailing edge, its rearmost point. Nearly every other aerofoil measurement — camber, thickness, angle of attack — is defined relative to this same line.

question: A wing's "taper ratio" — the ratio of tip chord to root chord — being less than 1, giving a tapered wing, mainly:

options.text: Increases structural weight compared with a rectangular wing of the same span and area
Reduces structural weight and can improve the spanwise lift distribution, though too much taper can promote earlier tip stall
Has no effect on stall behaviour whatsoever
Always eliminates wingtip vortices entirely

explanation: Tapering a wing concentrates structural material and bending load nearer the root, saving weight, and moves the lift distribution closer to the ideal elliptical shape. Taken too far, however, a heavily tapered tip carries a disproportionate share of lift at a given angle of attack and can stall before the root.

subtopic: Aspect Ratio and Lift Curve Slope
question: Independent of its effect on induced drag, increasing a wing's aspect ratio also:

options.text: Flattens the lift curve, so a larger change in angle of attack is needed for a given change in lift coefficient
Steepens the lift curve slope, so a smaller change in angle of attack produces a given change in lift coefficient, with CLmax typically reached at a lower angle of attack
Has no effect on the lift curve at all, only on drag
Makes the lift curve slope negative

explanation: A high aspect ratio wing behaves closer to an idealised two-dimensional aerofoil, giving it a steeper lift-curve slope than a low aspect ratio wing of the same section — a separate effect from aspect ratio's better-known influence on induced drag.

question: Compared with a high aspect ratio wing, a low aspect ratio wing (such as a delta planform) typically:

options.text: Stalls at a lower angle of attack, with a sharper, more sudden break
Reaches its maximum lift coefficient at a considerably higher angle of attack, with a more gradual, gentler stall
Has an identical lift curve slope to a high aspect ratio wing
Cannot generate lift at high angles of attack at all

explanation: A low aspect ratio wing's shallower lift curve slope means angle of attack has to rise much further before CLmax is reached, and the resulting stall tends to be more gradual — one reason delta-winged aircraft can be flown to very high angles of attack.

question: Reynolds number, as applied to airflow over an aerofoil, is best described as:

options.text: A ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces in the flow, increasing with airspeed, chord length and air density, and decreasing with air viscosity
A direct measure of an aerofoil's camber
Another name for aspect ratio
A fixed constant that never changes for a given aerofoil shape

explanation: Reynolds number compares the inertial and viscous forces acting in a flow. It rises with airspeed, chord length and density and falls with viscosity, and it governs whether a boundary layer behaves more like the smaller, slower flows tested in some wind tunnels or the large, fast flows of a real aircraft.

question: Increasing Reynolds number — for example, through higher airspeed or a larger chord — other factors unchanged, generally:

options.text: Decreases the maximum lift coefficient achievable
Increases the maximum lift coefficient achievable, since a relatively more energetic boundary layer resists separation to a higher angle of attack
Has no relationship to boundary layer behaviour at all
Only has an effect on aerofoils designed for supersonic flight

explanation: At a higher Reynolds number the boundary layer tends to transition to turbulent flow sooner and carries more energy relative to viscous losses, letting it withstand an adverse pressure gradient to a higher angle of attack before separating — which generally raises the achievable maximum lift coefficient.

subtopic: Aerodynamic Center vs Center of Pressure
question: Unlike the center of pressure, about which the pitching moment is always zero by definition, the pitching moment coefficient about the aerodynamic center:

options.text: Is also always zero at every angle of attack
Is essentially constant but generally non-zero — nose-down, for a conventional cambered aerofoil — across the linear range of angles of attack
Increases linearly with angle of attack in the same way the lift coefficient does
Is undefined for a symmetrical aerofoil

explanation: The center of pressure is, by definition, the point where the resultant force acts, so the moment about it is always zero — but that point moves with angle of attack. The aerodynamic center is instead defined as the point where the moment coefficient stays essentially constant, and for a cambered section that constant value is typically a small nose-down moment, not zero.

question: Extending trailing-edge flaps increases a wing section's effective camber, which typically:

options.text: Reduces the nose-down pitching moment about the aerodynamic center
Increases the nose-down pitching moment about the aerodynamic center, requiring a trim change
Has no effect on pitching moment, only on lift
Always produces a nose-up pitching moment, on every aircraft type

explanation: Adding camber with flaps shifts the load rearward on the wing section, increasing the nose-down pitching moment about the aerodynamic center. This is why extending or retracting flaps calls for a noticeable trim change.

question: Extending flaps typically changes an aerofoil section's lift characteristics by:

options.text: Increasing the maximum lift coefficient while decreasing the angle of attack at which the stall occurs
Decreasing the maximum lift coefficient while increasing the stalling angle of attack
Leaving both maximum lift coefficient and stalling angle of attack unchanged
Increasing both the maximum lift coefficient and the stalling angle of attack

explanation: Flaps raise the maximum lift coefficient available, which is exactly why they allow a lower approach and landing speed, but the added camber also means the section reaches that higher CLmax — and stalls — at a lower angle of attack than the clean wing does.

question: An elliptical wing planform is theoretically significant because, for a given aspect ratio, it produces:

options.text: The most concentrated lift distribution possible, peaking sharply at the wingtips
A uniform, elliptical spanwise lift distribution that minimises induced drag, though its tendency to stall across the whole span at once gives little stall warning
Zero induced drag under all flight conditions
A stall that always begins at the wing root first

explanation: An elliptical planform gives the theoretically ideal, uniform spanwise lift distribution for minimum induced drag at a given aspect ratio. Its drawback is that, because every section reaches its local CLmax at nearly the same angle of attack, the whole span tends to stall almost simultaneously, giving little pre-stall aileron buffet or asymmetry to warn the pilot.

question: A simple rectangular wing planform, compared with a tapered or elliptical one, typically stalls:

options.text: At the wingtips first, with early loss of aileron control
At the wing root first, which provides useful pre-stall buffet warning while the ailerons near the tips remain effective for longer
Simultaneously across the entire span, with no warning at all
Only at the trailing edge, never starting from the leading edge

explanation: A rectangular wing's local lift coefficient is higher toward the root than the tip at a given angle of attack, so the root reaches its stalling angle first. Turbulent, separated airflow off the root then buffets the tail before the tips — and their ailerons — actually stall.

question: A significant hazard of a swept-wing planform is that, owing to spanwise airflow toward the tips, the wing tends to stall:

options.text: At the root first, which is generally beneficial to controllability
At the wingtips first, which can produce a nose-up pitching tendency and an early loss of aileron control at the stall
Only at very low altitude
Only when the flaps are extended

explanation: Sweep encourages the boundary layer to drift spanwise toward the tips, thickening it there and promoting an earlier tip stall. Losing lift at the tips, which sit behind the center of gravity on a swept wing, tends to pitch the nose further up and can strip aileron effectiveness right when it is most needed.

question: "Washout" — a geometric or aerodynamic twist that reduces angle of attack toward the wingtip — is built into a wing primarily to:

options.text: Deliberately increase induced drag
Ensure the wing root reaches its stalling angle of attack before the tips do, preserving aileron control and giving useful stall warning
Increase the wingtip's angle of attack relative to the root
Reduce the wing's overall maximum lift coefficient

explanation: By fixing the tip at a lower angle of attack than the root, washout ensures the root stalls first regardless of planform, giving the same benefit a rectangular planform gives naturally — a controllable, forewarned stall rather than a sudden loss of aileron authority at the tips.

question: Leading-edge slats or slots increase maximum lift coefficient and delay the stall to a higher angle of attack mainly by:

options.text: Increasing the wing's total area
Directing a high-energy jet of air over the upper surface, re-energising the boundary layer so it resists separation for longer
Reducing the wing's camber
Increasing the wing's aspect ratio

explanation: A slat opens a gap ahead of the leading edge that accelerates air from the high-pressure lower surface over the upper surface, injecting extra energy into the boundary layer there. That re-energised layer withstands a steeper adverse pressure gradient before separating, pushing both CLmax and the stalling angle higher.

question: The critical (stalling) angle of attack for a given aerofoil and configuration:

options.text: Increases as airspeed increases
Is essentially constant regardless of airspeed, weight or bank angle — it is the speed at which CLmax's angle of attack is reached that varies, not the angle itself
Decreases as weight increases
Depends mainly on altitude, not on the aerofoil's shape

explanation: For a fixed configuration, the aerofoil always stalls at the same angle of attack — a property of the shape and the boundary layer, not of speed or weight. What changes with weight or load factor is the speed at which that fixed angle of attack, and its accompanying maximum lift coefficient, is reached.

question: In a four-digit NACA aerofoil designation, the digits describe, in order:

options.text: Wingspan, aspect ratio, and taper ratio
Maximum camber as a percentage of chord, the chordwise position of maximum camber, and maximum thickness as a percentage of chord
Aircraft weight category, engine type, and maximum design speed
The thickness ratio, repeated in three different units

explanation: A four-digit NACA number such as 2412 packs three geometric facts into its digits: 2% maximum camber, located at 40% of the chord, on a section 12% thick relative to its chord — a compact way of specifying an aerofoil's basic shape.

question: Toward the rear portion of an aerofoil's upper surface, static pressure typically begins rising again in the direction of flow — an adverse pressure gradient. This matters because:

options.text: It accelerates the boundary layer further, delaying separation indefinitely
It works against the boundary layer's remaining momentum and, if strong enough, causes the flow to separate from the surface
It only ever occurs on symmetrical aerofoils
It has no relationship to flow separation

explanation: Air accelerates and static pressure falls over the front part of an aerofoil, then decelerates and pressure rises again toward the trailing edge. That rising pressure pushes back against the boundary layer, and if the layer cannot fight through it, the flow separates — the mechanism that ultimately limits how high an angle of attack the section can sustain.

question: By convention, a pitching moment that tends to raise the nose (increase angle of attack) is described as:

options.text: Negative
Positive
Neutral
Undefined

explanation: By the standard sign convention, a nose-up pitching moment is positive and a nose-down one is negative. A conventional cambered aerofoil's pitching moment about its aerodynamic center is normally negative — nose-down — which is why the previous point about a reflex trailing edge and the horizontal tailplane both matter.
